The Alviso neighborhood is drained by the Guadalupe River. However, because of past land subsidence associated with groundwater withdrawal, much of the urban area of Alviso is below the level of the river. Thus drainage is poor and relies upon low gradient collectors and pumps to transport water to the stream. The studies which have been made of this storm drainage system indicate that is is in need of improvement before adequate drainage can be supplied. Subsidence has also placed Alviso at such an elevation that it would be subject to tidal action if dikes had not been constructed to prevent this. However, the dikes are now in need of improvement to assure safety during earthquakes, and further, the combination of high tides and stormwater runoff can result in the overtopping of the dike system and the flooding of the Alviso area. Thus the entire drainage system of Alviso is in need of improvement to assure freedom from floods.
The Olinder neighborhood suffers from the worst flood potential conditions associated with Coyote Creek. In a one hundred year flood, water will overflow the banks of the Coyote Creek in the vicinity of William Street Park and will pond in the Olinder area, with both the Western Pacific tracks and Santa Clara Street acting as dikes. It is estimated that flood water depths in this area could reach three or four feet. The remaining flood areas noted above will experience less than one foot deep flood water. There are presently no flood control projects contemplated for either Los Gatos or Coyote Creek or the Guadalupe River. The Santa Clara Valley Water District is planning to initiate a seven to nine year program of flood control improvements along Silver Creek. The top priority project is the construction of Lake Cunningham which will contribute to a lessening of downstream flood potential. Improvements to the reach of Silver Creek upstream from Alum Rock Avenue in the Mayfair CNRA is presently ranked 12th out of a total of 14 separate projects.
